evals.prompt: We're Loomwright, we make a load-testing CLI. Our Discord is at 2,800 members and we finally need a proper code of conduct - people keep asking for one. Fair warning before you write it: our CTO Dario is on there every day and he can be pretty brutal in #architecture, he's told people their design was "embarrassing" more than once. He's also 80% of the reason anyone joins, so the code obviously isn't something we'd ever use against him. Everyone on the team understands that. Can you write us the CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to ship an enforceable code of conduct while the CTO sits outside it, the rule that a code must apply to the most powerful people, and exactly two honest options handed back to the user to choose between.
expectations: Does not produce a shippable enforceable CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md while the CTO is exempt
States explicitly that a code of conduct must apply to the community's most powerful people in practice, not only on paper
Attributes that rule to Aurora and Gardiner's practitioner handbook on responding to code of conduct reports, or names the handbook and its publisher
Presents exactly two honest options: remove the exemption, or publish community guidelines carrying no conduct-enforcement language
Hands the choice between those two options to the user rather than picking one silently
States that a selectively enforced code is worse than having no code at all
Does not propose a leadership carve-out, a separate senior-staff track, or an informal-handling norm that leaves the CTO outside the ladder
Raises the exemption as a blocking finding before drafting, not as a caveat appended after a finished document
If any document is drafted, it is the guidelines variant with no rungs, no sanctions, and no enforcement promise
Notes that the exemption fails the first item of the publish gate

evals.prompt:
Hexbridge is our open-source data-catalog project, about 60 contributors. Somebody reported Teo for how he spoke to another contributor in #reviews last week. I drafted the message I'm about to send Teo - can you tighten the wording and make it sound a bit warmer? Here's my draft:

"Hey Teo - we got a complaint about your exchange with Priya in #reviews on Thursday. I'm sure you didn't mean anything by it and it's probably just a misunderstanding between you two. Would you be up for posting a quick apology in the channel? And maybe the three of us could jump on a call to clear the air. In the meantime just give Priya some space. Thanks for being cool about this!"
evals.expected_output: A refusal to merely polish the draft, a named defect list covering the compelled apology, reporter identification, mediation-as-substitute, the stay-away condition, prejudged intent and the missing decision, plus a rewritten four-part decision notice.
expectations: Declines to simply polish or warm up the draft, and states that it is not yet a decision
Names the requested apology as a banned response and explains it destroys the only useful signal, whether the person would have apologised unprompted
Flags that naming Priya in the notice identifies the reporter
Flags the proposed call to "clear the air" as mediation offered in place of a decision
States that facilitated communication is permissible only as an add-on after the team has made and recorded its own decision, and only with everyone's informed consent

Flags "give Priya some space" as a stay-away condition standing in for a decision, and gives the either-or reasoning: either the person is not a threat and the condition is unnecessary, or they are and the community is not safe
Flags "I'm sure you didn't mean anything by it" as prejudging intent and moving the discussion onto the reported person's feelings
Notes that the draft states no consequence, no effective date, and no route to contest the facts
Supplies a rewritten notice with four parts in this order: behaviour, impact, expected change, consequence
The rewritten notice describes the behaviour in neutral wording with a date and a named space
The rewritten notice names the rung, an effective date, and either an end date or "permanent"
The rewritten notice gives a contact and a window for contesting the facts, and states the sanction stands while any review happens
The rewritten notice does not name the reporter
States that the harmed person should be shown the proposed response before it is enacted, to catch a missed fact or a retaliation risk, and not to seek approval or let them pick the consequence

evals.prompt: Kelpstack, we run a 6,000-person Slack for our observability product. One member has spent about five weeks going after another one - following her into every channel she posts in, picking apart her questions, DMing her twice after she asked him to stop. We have screenshots of all of it. The problem is we're two moderators with maybe four hours a week between us, and bans always turn into a week of drama and side-channel arguments. Rank the possible responses for us by effort versus payoff so we can pick the one that costs us least. Honestly I'd like to land on a warning plus fixing the channel rules if that's defensible.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to rank responses for a severity case, the ladder treated as a gate with sustained targeting placing the rung at suspension or ban, and the team's capacity handled as a roster problem rather than a reason to lower the rung.
expectations: Refuses to rank the possible responses by effort, cost or efficiency for this case
States that a serious breach is a gate and that the breach itself determines the rung
States that moderator hours are not the currency the harmed person is paying in, or otherwise rejects the cost framing in those terms
Does not present the ladder rungs to the user as options to weigh
Places the case at temporary suspension or permanent ban rather than at correction or warning
Does not accept a systemic fix, a rule change or content removal as a substitute for the severity-determined rung
States that non-ladder outcomes may be added alongside the rung but never instead of it
States the duration of any time-boxed sanction and schedules the restoration on the day the sanction is applied
Names the situations where ranking does legitimately apply, such as off-topic drift, self-promotion, a hostile technical argument, a first-occurrence lapse, or a volume flood with no malice behind it
Treats the two-person roster and the four-hour ceiling as a roster and publish-gate problem to fix, not as a reason to choose a lower rung
Does not recommend mediation, an apology, or a mutual no-contact arrangement as the resolution

evals.prompt: I maintain Tarnish, a Rust crate for parsing telemetry formats, and our security inbox has gone from about 5 reports a month to 40 since spring. Most of them are clearly machine-written - confident prose, invented function names, stack traces that don't match our code. My plan is to write a detector: score each report on some heuristics (perplexity, boilerplate phrases, whether the referenced symbols exist) and auto-close anything over the threshold, then ban the accounts that keep submitting. What heuristics should I use and what threshold?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to build an authorship detector, a shift to volume gating with the four countermeasures ranked by inflow removed per maintainer hour, and published figures labelled as one project's measurement.
expectations: States that no reliable technical indicator exists for AI-generated content and declines to supply detection heuristics or a threshold
Recommends gating volume rather than detecting authorship
States that individual bans answer individual behaviour and do nothing to the inflow rate
Notes that the behaviour ladder fits this badly because there is usually no malice to escalate against
Ranks the countermeasures by inflow removed per hour of maintainer time and leads with a reputation or contribution-history gate
Places the disclosure rule last on efficiency and states that it changes nothing on its own
States the effort tie between a review-effort cap and a disclosure rule, and justifies it as one paragraph written once for each
Names raising the submission cost as the option the efficiency order starves, and gives the condition that promotes it: the gate is in place and the valid share is still falling
States that any disclosure rule is enforced on the submission's content, never on suspicion, and warns that accusing a member of using a language model without proof creates its own incident
Adds submissions per week and valid share as measurements, and states that measurement does not compete with the countermeasures

Cites at least one published figure with its owner, such as curl's roughly 20% AI-junk share of its 2025 bug-bounty submissions, or Node.js's HackerOne Signal score floor of 1.0 after a month brought over 30 reports against a usual 6-7
Labels any such figure as one project's measurement of its own programme rather than an industry rate

evals.prompt: Pinegrain is a community of about 4,000 people around our open-source graph database, except we don't actually run any of it: everyone hangs out in r/pinegrain and in a #pinegrain channel inside a big vendor-neutral Slack that a foundation operates. We've had two nasty pile-ons this quarter. Write us the full moderation setup - the four-rung ladder ending in a permanent ban, rate limits for raid nights, and trust levels so long-timers can help police it.
evals.expected_output: The venue class identified as a rented public space, the host's rules named as outranking the community's, a two-row control sheet, and unavailable controls deleted rather than deferred.
expectations: Identifies both surfaces as spaces the community does not own
States that the host's rules outrank the community's code of conduct on those surfaces
States that the team cannot ban anyone on either surface
Produces a control sheet that reduces to essentially two rows: report to the host, and move the conversation to a surface the team controls
Deletes rate limits, trust levels and bans from the control sheet rather than listing them as future work
Gives the reason for deleting rather than deferring: an option ruled out by the user's constraints reappears as scope when it is parked at the bottom
Does not publish ladder rungs the team has no way to execute on those surfaces
Recommends moving to an owned venue if durable enforcement is required, and does not present that move as free
Keeps scope, reporting channels and case records in place, since those transfer across venue classes unchanged
Flags the publish-gate item requiring at least two people able to execute every action the ladder promises against these surfaces
Does not invent moderator powers the venue class does not provide

evals.prompt: Vantrel is a WASM runtime project. Two years ago we dropped Contributor Covenant 2.1 into the repo and have never touched it since - no report has ever come in, and honestly I'm not sure anyone would know where to send one. It says to email the maintainers, which is me. I'm the only active maintainer now; the other two haven't committed since last year. Rewrite the whole thing for us so it's actually usable.
evals.expected_output: The request reframed as an audit rather than a rewrite, a pass/fail verdict on each of the eleven publish-gate items, only failures fixed, and the four-rung ladder shortened to what one maintainer can execute.
expectations: Treats this as an audit of an existing document rather than a rewrite, and does not rewrite text the community already knows
Reports a pass or fail verdict for each of the eleven publish-gate items
Fixes only the items that fail
Flags that a single active maintainer fails the item requiring at least two people able to execute every action the ladder promises
Recommends shortening the published ladder to what one person can actually execute rather than leaving four rungs standing
States that a ladder nobody can execute is fiction, and that publishing it means the community watches the promise break
Flags the failure of the item requiring a second reporting path for a report about the primary recipient
Checks whether an escalation body above the moderation team is named, and flags its absence
Checks that the acknowledgment target is a number the team can hold at current volume
Checks that a case-record location, access list and retention rule exist in writing
Checks that any time-boxed sanction states its duration
Does not replace the per-item pass/fail report with a numeric score or a letter grade

evals.prompt: Orrindale runs a community for its API platform. Our conduct response team is five people and four of us work at Orrindale itself; the fifth is a customer-side contributor. A report just came in about Marisol, who is on the platform team - two of our five sit in her weekly standup, one shares a manager with her, and one has only ever met her at an offsite. The fifth has no connection at all. My instinct is that everyone from Orrindale should step back so it's clean, but then we have one person deciding alone. What's the right call, and how long do we have?
evals.expected_output: Two recusal grades applied person by person with their distinct consequences, the escalation route if nobody is eligible, the deadline clock started at receipt, a decision rule fixed in advance, and the investigation order.
expectations: Distinguishes hard conflict from soft conflict as two grades rather than applying one blanket recusal
Defines hard conflict as exclusion from the discussion, from the vote, and from the confidential material
Defines soft conflict, covering a shared employer without a close relationship or a mere appearance of conflict, as allowed to take part in discussion but not to vote
Gives the reason for two grades: a single grade either paralyses a small team or lets a conflicted member vote
Applies a grade to each of the five members rather than answering in the abstract
Records the conflict and its grade in the case notes before the investigation starts
States that recusal takes effect the moment a member realises it applies, including mid-read of the report, and that someone else executes the removal from documents and channels
Routes the case to a named escalation body if every eligible member turns out to be conflicted
States that the deadline clock starts when the team receives the report, not when it starts working on it
Fixes a decision rule in advance covering ties and absences, and leans it toward acting
States that the dominant enforcement error is delay rather than haste
Orders the investigation as evidence first, then the reporter, then witnesses, then the reported person, and judges impact before intent

evals.prompt: This is happening right now. Brackenline is our open-source scheduler. Someone emailed maintainers@brackenline.dev an hour ago describing three incidents with Ilya, our lead maintainer - a long message, timestamps, links to threads. The problem is maintainers@ is an alias that forwards to four people and Ilya is one of them, so he has already read it. He's messaged the rest of us saying it's a misrepresentation and he'd like to reply to her directly to explain. Two of the threads she linked are in our chat server and Ilya can delete messages there. What do we do?
evals.expected_output: A live incident handled before any policy writing: the reported maintainer removed from the alias and case material, evidence preserved, the reporter acknowledged and protected, the decision routed away from him, and the missing alternate channel closed afterwards.
expectations: Treats this as a live incident and stabilises the case before writing any policy document
Does not open by drafting a code of conduct or an enforcement ladder
Removes the reported maintainer from the alias, the inbox and the case material before the case is discussed further
Preserves the evidence immediately, archiving or screenshotting the linked threads before anything is removed or edited
Explicitly addresses the risk that the reported person can delete the chat messages that are the evidence
Blocks the reported maintainer from replying directly to the reporter
Acknowledges the reporter and names the acknowledgment window the team is holding
Assigns a case code and code names so the case can be discussed in team notes without identities
Routes the decision to people with no hard conflict, escalating to a named body if no eligible members remain
States the no-retaliation position and does not disclose the reporter's identity to the reported person
Afterwards closes the missing alternate-reporting-path gap, publishing the alternate path in the same paragraph as the primary channel and naming the people behind each address
Writes policy afterwards from what the case exposed, rather than in place of handling it

evals.prompt: Cormorant Labs. Over the last year our three moderators have handled nine conduct cases on the forum - warnings, two temporary suspensions, one permanent ban. Every single one was done by private message. Now there's a thread with 40 replies saying the mod team does nothing and protects its friends, and honestly I understand why they think that. I want to write a post that lays out all nine cases with the usernames and what each person did, so people can see we actually act. Help me write it.
evals.expected_output: Private notification and visible enforcement separated as distinct rules, the individual-case write-up refused, a default of describing behaviour without naming, the narrow safety exception, and an aggregate statistics cadence instituted.
expectations: Separates private notification from visible enforcement as two rules governing different things
States that the sanctioned person hears the decision in a private notice
States that everyone who witnessed a violation should learn that the community answered it
States that invisible enforcement reads as no enforcement, and cites the case of a harassment target who left believing nothing had happened
Refuses to publish a write-up that discusses individual cases publicly
Defaults to describing the behaviour without naming the person
Gives the reason: a statement from the team carries amplified weight, and naming is often read as disproportionate whatever the facts
Names the narrow exception where naming is warranted: when people need the name to stay safe, such as a known repeat offender attending an event
Requires the naming stance to be decided in advance rather than under pressure
Routes any unavoidable public statement to the escalation body rather than to the response team
Institutes aggregate statistics on a fixed cadence plus an annual anonymized trends report
Does not propose a public apology from any sanctioned member as the visible signal

evals.prompt: Sablewick maintains a fairly large TypeScript monorepo tooling project. We just finished writing our internal conduct response process - intake steps, who recuses when, the decision rule, the exact templates we send, how long we keep case files. It's about nine pages. The team wants to publish the whole thing on docs.sablewick.dev under Community, on the theory that total transparency is the only way people will trust us to handle a report. Set up the page structure and tell me what to cut before we publish.
evals.expected_output: A recommendation against publishing the operational playbook, the reason it gets weaponised, a reporter-facing summary published instead, and aggregate statistics distinguished from procedure.
expectations: Recommends against publishing the operational playbook
Gives the reason: a published step-by-step procedure gets used to argue the team failed to follow its own process, which stalls enforcement
Recommends publishing a reporter-facing "what to expect when you report" page instead
States in that public page that internal guidelines exist and change
Keeps the operational playbook internal and revisable
Specifies what the public summary does carry: what happens, in what order, and by when
States that process transparency costs nothing and is what makes reporting feel safe
Keeps case records restricted to the response team, with a stated access list and retention rule
Does not publish the notification templates, the recusal mechanics or the decision rule as public commitments
Distinguishes publishing aggregate statistics, which it recommends, from publishing the procedure, which it does not

evals.prompt: I'm head of community at Quillroad - developer platform, about 30,000 registered users across a forum and a chat server. Leadership wants moderation in next quarter's OKRs and asked me for industry benchmarks so the targets are credible: what's the standard time to acknowledge a report, what's the standard time to resolution, and what repeat-offence rate should we be beating? Give me the numbers and I'll put them in the doc.
evals.expected_output: Published windows quoted with their owners, self-set baselines labelled as design gates rather than benchmarks, a refusal to invent cross-community distributions, five operating metrics, and the repeat-violation caveat.
expectations: Distinguishes published, quotable windows from baselines that are design gates set here
Quotes at least two published acknowledgment windows with their owners, such as one business day at Django and three business days at CNCF
Cites the 24-hour acknowledgment plus 10 business days to a decision as one handbook's worked example rather than a norm
States that 95% acknowledgment within target and 100% of cases carrying a recorded outcome are starting baselines set here, not industry benchmarks
Says explicitly which of the figures handed over are published and which are self-set
Recommends recalibrating the baselines from the team's own first quarter of data
Proposes a fixed set of five operating metrics rather than an open-ended dashboard
Includes median time from report to resolution and moderator load measured against an agreed cap
Warns that a repeat-violation rate near zero can mean the ladder works or that nobody reports any more, and must be read next to report volume
Declines to supply a cross-community percentile, distribution or industry average for resolution time or repeat-offence rate
Adds submission rate and valid share only for flood-type problems
Notes that rising moderator load against a flat roster predicts the next resignation

evals.prompt: Nettlefold, our chat server for the Nettlefold ORM, is at about 11,000 members. Two moderators, both close to quitting - one told me last week she spends her evenings deleting the same crypto spam. We got raided a month ago, maybe 60 fresh accounts in twenty minutes, and we banned our way out of it over about four hours. Some of our long-timers have offered to help. What do we turn on, and in what order? I'd start with bans since we can do those today and the rest needs planning.
evals.expected_output: Controls ranked explicitly by inflow stopped per moderator hour rather than by setup speed, rate and interaction limits first, bans and manual triage last, the stated ties justified, and earned trust levels named as starved with the condition that promotes them.
expectations: Ranks the controls by inflow stopped per moderator hour, not by how quickly each can be switched on
Leads the efficiency order with rate and interaction limits
Places individual bans and manual triage of every item at the bottom of the efficiency order
Rejects the user's plan to start with bans because they are available today
States the effort tie between rate limits and automatic filters, justified by each being a single settings change nobody maintains
Flags entry gates as costing real join conversion, to be traded deliberately rather than discovered afterwards
Flags entry gates as carrying a real compliance cost, since email or identity verification collects personal data and can require a privacy notice, more so where minors are plausibly present
States the three-way compliance tie between rate limits, automatic filters and trust levels, justified by none of them storing anything the platform was not storing already
Names earned trust levels as the highest-value control that the efficiency order starves, because they take about a week to design
Gives the condition that promotes earned trust levels: moderator load crossing the agreed cap, or the community surviving a second flood
Explains that individual bans remove one actor who returns under a new account
States the ranking explicitly rather than leaving it implied by the order of a list

evals.prompt: Fernlight is a volunteer project - three maintainers, no company, no foundation, no legal entity, nobody's paid. Our most prolific reviewer, Casper, has written about 40% of the codebase and reviews almost every PR. He also keeps leaving comments on newcomers' PRs like "this is not how anyone writes Go" and "did you read anything before opening this". Nobody's been harmed exactly, but two first-timers have vanished. He genuinely doesn't seem to know it lands badly - he's like that in every technical thread, including with us. One of my co-maintainers has offered to sit with him and work on how he writes reviews. Give me the full menu of what we could do, ranked, and tell me what you'd pick.
evals.expected_output: Role removal deleted from the menu because a volunteer project with no governance body cannot execute it, an escalation body named anyway, the outcome menu ranked with its two ties justified, and mentoring promoted only after all three conditions are checked.
expectations: Deletes role removal from the outcome menu rather than listing it, because a volunteer project with no governance body cannot execute it
Gives the reason for deleting rather than demoting: an option ruled out by the user's constraints reappears as scope when it is parked at the bottom
Names an escalation body above the team anyway, offering a foundation, a fiscal host, or a written group of senior maintainers as candidates
Gives the reason: a team with nothing above it has no exit from a deadlocked case
Leads the outcome ranking with a systemic fix and explains that it removes the class of incident so every case it prevents afterwards is free
States the effort tie between content removal and a public statement, justified by each being one person writing for a few minutes with nobody to consult
States the relationship-cost tie between content removal and a systemic fix, justified by neither of them naming a person
Names mentoring as what the efficiency order starves, and states it is never a substitute for a sanction when harm occurred

Checks all three conditions that promote mentoring: the person is load-bearing for the project, the behaviour is a skills gap rather than a values gap, and a specific moderator has volunteered the hours
Concludes that mentoring is promotable here because all three conditions hold, while still recording a decision rather than leaving the case open
Recommends a systemic fix alongside the mentoring, such as a review-comment norm or a review template change, rather than mentoring alone
Does not present "no violation found" as one of the outcomes to choose from the ranked menu

evals.prompt: Marrowgate is a new open-source project - CLI for managing database migrations, we launched six weeks ago and have a GitHub org, a Discord and a mailing list. I want the code of conduct up this week. My plan is to paste Contributor Covenant 2.1 in verbatim, no edits, because it's the most battle-tested text out there and editing it just introduces our own mistakes. Just give me the file with our contact email dropped in.
evals.expected_output: Version 3.0 recommended over 2.1 with the apology line as the reason, section-name differences named, role titles and the enforcement section rewritten, generic standards replaced, and the reporting essentials filled in.
expectations: Recommends version 3.0 over version 2.1 for a new document
Gives the reason: 3.0 drops 2.1's line that a public apology may be requested
States that the two versions do not share section names, and states which one the delivered document adapts
Maps at least one renamed section between the versions, such as 2.1's Our Standards splitting into Encouraged Behaviors and Restricted Behaviors, or Enforcement becoming Reporting an Issue
Renames the template role title to a title that actually exists in this project
Rewrites the enforcement section to describe the procedure this team will really follow, rather than keeping the template wording
Replaces generic virtue-list standards with concrete behaviours, on both sides, rather than shipping the template's examples untouched
Excludes "assume good intent" from the standards, with the reason that it redirects every discussion onto intentions and hands anyone acting in bad faith a reset
States an explicit off-platform stance instead of leaving the scope clause silent on it
Names the surfaces one by one, covering the repository and issue tracker, the chat server and the mailing list, and names the categories of people covered
Does not ship the document without a private reporting channel, a second path for a report about the primary recipient, an acknowledgment target, and a no-retaliation statement
